prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, Nobody, Math

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of the text, preserving its content, tone, and recurring refrain while refining the language for greater eloquence:

---

I am fourteen, and my skin has betrayed me. The boy I cannot live without still secretly sucks his thumb. Why must my knees always look so ashen? What if I should die before morning—and Momma is in the bedroom with the door closed.

I must learn to dance in time for the next party; my room feels far too small for who I am. Suppose I die before graduation—they will sing mournful songs, yet finally speak the truth about me. There is nothing I wish to do, and far too much that must be done—and Momma is in the bedroom with the door closed.

No one ever pauses to consider my side of things. I should have made the Math Team; my grades were better than his. Why must I be the one stuck wearing braces? I have nothing to wear tomorrow. Will I even live long enough to grow up?—and Momma is in the bedroom with the door closed.

---

Let me know if you'd like a version with a different tone—more formal, more lyrical, or closer to free verse structure.
outputs.L2: At fourteen, my complexion has turned against me — the boy I'm hopelessly devoted to still secretly sucks his thumb. Why are my knees perpetually dry and ashen? What happens if I don't wake up tomorrow, while mom stays shut away in her room. I need to figure out dancing before the upcoming party — my bedroom feels too cramped for me. What if I don't make it to graduation? They'll perform mournful songs, but at least they'll finally speak honestly about who I was. There's nothing I feel like doing, yet so much demands to be done, and mom remains behind that closed bedroom door. No one bothers to consider things from my perspective — I deserved a spot on the Math Team since my grades outshone his. Why am I the one stuck with braces? I've got nothing decent to wear, and will I even survive long enough to reach adulthood, while mom stays isolated in her room with the door shut.
outputs.L3:
**Fourteen**

I am fourteen years old and I am falling apart in all the usual places. My skin has betrayed me overnight, blooming red and angry across my forehead like it's trying to say something my mouth can't. My knees are ashy no matter how much lotion I steal from the bathroom cabinet, gray and dry like they belong to someone else, someone older, someone who has stopped caring. And my teeth—my teeth are the wrong shape, crowded together like they're trying to escape my mouth, and everyone keeps saying *braces, you'll need braces* like it's a sentence being handed down.

At night I lie in bed and think about dying. Not in some dramatic way, not with any real understanding of what that means, but as a small persistent hum beneath everything else. What if I don't wake up tomorrow. What if I die before I walk across that stage at graduation, before I even get the chance to become whatever it is I'm supposed to become. What if I never get to grow up at all, and all of this—the skin, the knees, the teeth—was for nothing, wasted worry spent on a body that wouldn't even get the chance to be embarrassed by itself for very long.

And then there's the Math Team. I should have made it. I know the material better than Sarah does, I know it, but she got the spot and I didn't, and nobody said anything about it being unfair because apparently only I noticed. Apparently only I keep score.

My mother's door is closed again. It has been closed more often than open lately, a thin white barrier between her room and the hallway where I stand sometimes, just standing there, not knocking, not sure what I would even say if I did. I don't know what she does in there. I don't ask. The door stays closed through dinner, through the hours after, through the mornings when I leave for school without saying goodbye because saying goodbye to a closed door feels like talking to no one.

There's a party coming up and I don't know how to dance and I don't have anything to wear, and these two facts sit in my chest with the same weight as everything else, the same weight as dying before morning, the same weight as the door that stays closed. I don't know how to explain to anyone that all of it feels equally urgent—the skin, the knees, the teeth, the unfairness, the closed door, the dance I don't know, the outfit I don't have. It all just piles up, unsorted, and I carry it around because there's no one to hand it to.

I am fourteen years old and I am waiting—for my skin to clear, for morning to come, for the door to open.
outputs.L4:
# Fourteen

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and there's a pimple on my chin the size of a planet
and Jimmy Sanchez looked at me today, or maybe
he looked at Ashley Kim standing behind me
and I can't tell if that's worse or better

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and I don't know how to move my hips
like the other girls do at recess when the radio plays
and my arms feel too long for my body
like they're borrowed from someone taller, someone
who knows what to do with them

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and grandpa's cough sounded different on the phone
wet in a way that scared me
and I lay awake wondering what happens
when we stop, just stop, like a clock
nobody winds anymore
and I am fourteen and I already know
that everything ends

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and it's not fair that Sarah gets to stay out till nine
and it's not fair that my thighs touch when I sit down
and it's not fair that some girls wake up
already knowing how to be beautiful
while I'm still practicing in the mirror
faces that might someday fit

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and I have this word stuck in my throat
it's small, it's just three letters
help
or maybe it's just
momma

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and I stand in the hallway
counting the seconds between
my heartbeat and my knock
that never comes

because some doors you learn
not to open
because some silences
teach you how to be quiet too

momma's in the bedroom with the door closed

and I am fourteen
and so much is happening
inside this skin, this heart,
this body becoming something
I don't recognize yet

and there is no one
to tell.
outputs.L5:
# There Was Nobody Good at Math

There was nobody in the room who claimed to be good at math, yet the whiteboard was covered in equations. It was a strange kind of humility—everyone downplaying their abilities while somehow producing a proof that would make a tenured professor nod in approval.

This is the paradox of mathematical confidence. Ask a room full of engineers, scientists, or even casual puzzle enthusiasts, and you'll often hear the same refrain: "Oh, I was never really good at math." Yet these are the same people who calculate tips instantly, spot patterns in data, or explain complex statistical concepts to their friends. Nobody wants to claim the title, but the skills are undeniably present.

Why does this happen? Perhaps it's because math, more than almost any other subject, carries the weight of comparison. There's always someone who can solve it faster, someone who intuitively grasps concepts that took you hours to understand. Against that backdrop, nobody feels quite adequate enough to claim expertise.

But maybe that's the wrong way to think about it. Being "good at math" isn't a fixed destination—it's a spectrum of understanding built through practice, mistakes, and slow revelation. Nobody starts out fluent in the language of numbers. Nobody skips the confusion, the wrong turns, the moments of staring blankly at a problem.

So the next time there is nobody in the room willing to claim mathematical confidence, remember: that same room is often filled with quiet capability, waiting to be acknowledged rather than dismissed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of a fourteen-year-old girl listing her everyday teenage worries alongside a recurring, more troubling refrain about her mother being shut away in her bedroom.
counterfactuals.output:
**Things I Think About Before First Period**

My hair won't sit right, it's doing that flip thing,
Sarah didn't like my post, just left it there, no heart,
I have a math test and I didn't study,
did I leave my retainer at Dad's again—

and Mom's been in her room since Tuesday.

Is my skirt too short, is my skirt too long,
does Jake think I'm funny or just weird,
I said something dumb at lunch on Monday,
everyone laughed but not with me, I think—

and the door's still closed, the blinds still down.

I need better shoes, mine look babyish,
I have to text back Emma but what do I even say,
there's a party Friday and I don't know
if I'm invited or just heard about—

and I brought her toast up, she said not hungry,
said maybe later, said turn off the light.

Did I do the reading, will she call on me,
my skin's doing that thing again, right on my chin,
I hope nobody saw me trip in the hallway,
I hope my voice didn't crack like that in choir—

and I stood outside her door and listened
and didn't hear anything at all.

I wish I was prettier, I wish I was smaller,
I wish Jake would just look at me once,
I have to pick a topic for my history project,
I have to remember gym clothes, I always forget—

and it's been six days now, maybe seven,
and I make my own lunch, I don't really mind,
and I tell my friends she's just got a headache,
a bad one, a long one, that's all that it is.

Did I brush my teeth, did I finish my homework,
is my life going to always feel like this,
small worries stacked up like books on a shelf,
and underneath them, holding up the whole thing—

the door. Still closed.
The light. Still off.
Her voice, when it comes, so far away,
like she's talking to me from underwater,
like she's already left and this is just an echo,

and I don't know what to do with that,
so I write down my homework,
so I pick out tomorrow's socks,
so I keep on living the small life,
the loud, small, everyday life,

right outside her door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create a spoken-word style poem, similar to Nikki Giovanni's writing, that mixes trivial adolescent anxieties with an undertone of family crisis, using a repeated line for structure?
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Worry About On Tuesdays

I worry about my hair on Tuesdays
whether the part is straight
whether the boy who sits behind me
in second period notices
that I re-curled it twice this morning

but this is not about my hair

I worry about my hair on Tuesdays
because Tuesday is the day
Daddy comes to get his mail
from the house he doesn't live in anymore
and Mama irons her blouse
like she's going somewhere
but she's not going anywhere
she's just standing in the kitchen
being ironed herself

I worry about my hair on Tuesdays
and whether I said something wrong
at lunch, whether Keisha's mad at me
for real or just quiet-mad
which is worse, which means
I have to guess
which is what I do at home too
guess whether the quiet
means everything's fine
or means get your book bag
and go to your room
and turn the music up

I worry about my hair on Tuesdays
I worry about the way
my brother's jaw gets tight
like he's chewing on something
that was never food
I worry about my grade in Geometry
and whether that's even
the kind of thing
a person's allowed to worry about
when there are boxes
in the hallway
that nobody's labeled yet

I worry about my hair on Tuesdays
because worrying about hair
is a door I can walk through
and shut behind me
because the other worry
doesn't have a door
it's just a house
getting quieter
and me
getting good
at holding my breath

I worry about my hair on Tuesdays
so I don't have to worry
that this Tuesday
might be the last one
Daddy comes at all
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem from a teen girl's perspective—she worries about acne, boys, dances, and grades, but keeps returning to the line "and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed."
counterfactuals.output:
**And Momma's in the Bedroom**

There's a zit on my chin the size of Texas
and I have this idea that if I just don't touch it
don't even look at it in the mirror
it might pack up and leave on its own,
find someone else's face to ruin,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

Jake Wheeler said hi to me in the hallway today
and I said hi back but it came out weird,
too high, like a question,
like I was asking him permission to exist,
and I've been replaying it for six hours now,
turning it over like a rock I can't put down,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

The Winter Formal is in nine days
and I don't have a date and I don't have a dress
and Britney already asked Marcus
which means the good boys are going fast
like bread at Thanksgiving,
and I keep telling myself it doesn't matter
but it matters, it matters so much
it's sitting on my chest like a stack of books,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

I got a C on the algebra test.
A C. Like the letter is laughing at me.
Dad's gonna ask about it at dinner,
if dad even remembers dinner is a thing that happens,
if dad even sits down anymore,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

She used to leave it open a crack,
just enough that I could hear the TV,
hear her laugh at something dumb,
hear her call out *supper's almost ready, baby*
but that was in the fall,
before the leaves finished falling,
before the phone calls got quiet and short,
before I learned to walk soft down that hallway
like the floor itself might break.

I worry about my skin.
I worry about boys who don't look at me
and the ones who look too long.
I worry about grades and dresses and being enough,
being enough, being enough—

but underneath all that worry,
folded up small so I don't have to hold it all at once,
there's this other thing,
this bigger thing,
this thing I don't have words for yet
except to say:

and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed,
and I stand outside it some nights,
my hand raised to knock,
and I don't.

I go back to my room.
I pick at my face in the mirror.
I text somebody about somebody.
I do my homework wrong on purpose
just to have something to fail at
that isn't this,
that isn't her,
that isn't the sound of nothing
coming from behind that door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem for a creative writing class that captures the chaotic inner monologue of a young girl balancing surface-level teenage problems with a deeper fear that something is wrong at home.
counterfactuals.output:
# What's Wrong With Me

Did Jessica see me trip in the hallway
did she tell Marcus did Marcus tell everyone
my hair looks stupid today stupid stupid
why did I wear this shirt

Dad's car wasn't in the driveway again
probably just working late working late working late
that's what Mom said last night too fast
too bright, like a light switched on wrong

I have a test tomorrow I haven't studied
I haven't studied because I can't
because the walls are so thin
and I heard something break at 2 AM

was it a plate

Sarah's having a party this weekend
everyone's invited except apparently me
did I do something wrong
am I too much am I not enough

Mom's been wearing sunglasses inside
which is weird right that's weird
but maybe it's a headache
maybe it's just a headache

I need new shoes everyone has the new shoes
I need to disappear into the carpet
when he raises his voice like that
over nothing, over dishes, over

nothing

My phone buzzed six times during class
probably nothing probably just the group chat
probably not Mom
probably not asking where I am
probably not asking me to hurry home

I picked at my nail polish until it bled
a little, just a little
I can control this
I can control the small things

the shirt, the hair, the test
the party I wasn't invited to
the sound of a car pulling in
too late, too quiet, too much like relief

I am fourteen and I am furious
about things that don't matter
because the things that matter
are too big to hold

so I hold the small ones instead
turn them over and over
like stones in my pocket
like something I can keep safe

---

*Feel free to adjust the age, specific details, or tone to match your character's voice—I can also revise for a different structure (more/less fragmented, rhyming, etc.) if that suits your assignment better.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem with a repeating refrain that contrasts silly teenage complaints (ashy knees, braces, party dances) with the ominous, unspoken reality of a mother isolating herself behind a closed door.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Mama Doesn't Say

My knees are ashy, chalk-white and rough,
I forgot the lotion, that's plenty enough
To ruin a Tuesday, to ruin my day—
But Mama's door is closed. She doesn't come out to play.

These braces cut my cheek when I try to smile,
Mr. Davis assigned homework, like, ten miles' worth of files,
Jasmine wore the same shirt as me, how uncool—
But Mama's door stays shut. She hasn't left for school.

I practiced that new dance for hours last night,
The one where you dip and you spin to the right,
Nobody noticed, nobody cared—
But Mama's light stays off. Nobody's asked how I've fared.

Braces, ashy knees, the whole world feels unfair,
I slam my door too, just to make it seem fair,
Like our two shut doors are the same kind of thing—
But mine opens by morning. Hers stays closed like a wing

Folded tight around something I can't see or name,
Some Tuesday that swallowed the girl she became.
I complain about small things, the silly, the loud—
While something in that room wears a heavier shroud.

Ashy knees. Broken braces. A missed silly dance.
These are the words I know, the ones I can chance
To say out loud, to make into noise—
While her silence gets bigger, and swallows her voice.

I knock sometimes. I leave her a plate.
I say I'm sorry for something. I don't know what. I wait.
The door stays a door. I go back to my day—
Ashy knees, broken braces—the things I can say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
